description: My technical interests include software development, AI, data analysis and problem-solving. I am always eager to experiment with ideas and challenge myself to build things beyond my comfort zone.
summary:
Burning Calendar is a harmonized fire record and an interactive web app. It combines 26 years of NASA FIRMS hotspots from MODIS (Terra, Aqua) and VIIRS (Suomi NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21) into one consistent monthly time series. It covers 50 Asian countries and Argentina also with their provinces and districts. The app shows each area as a year × month burning calendar with trends, unusual seasons, fire events followed day by day and short-term forecast.

MODIS and VIIRS are differ in pixel size (1 km vs 375 m), sensitivity and overpass time, so their records can't be compared directly. We convert every month to NOAA-20 terms with steps tested on years they never saw, and give each estimate an uncertainty range. The false +199 % jump in Asia's record at the 2012 switch becomes +2 %. The result agrees with NASA GFED5 burned area (r = 0.94 for Asia, 0.97 for Argentina).

Why it matters: Fire agencies, haze forecasters and researchers need long-term trends they can trust. Without harmonization, a change of satellite looks like a fire crisis.
details:
Burning Calendar turns 26 years of NASA fire detections from November 2000 to November 2026 into one consistent monthly record. The system covers about 85 million detections for 50 Asian countries and 5.6 million for Argentina. For 1,771 areas (continent, region, country, province or district), the web app shows:

- a fire map with year-by-year and month-by-month playback, and the latest detections

- a burning calendar (year × month) with each season compared against a typical year, and El Niño / La Niña years marked

- a consistency card proving the record has no false jumps when satellites change

- fire events: each fire followed day by day as ~1 km squares on the map, and ranked against earlier fires

- satellite photos before and after a fire, a short-wave infrared view that sees through smoke, and a daily haze and smoke layer

- a next-week and weeks 2–4 fire forecast, tested against simple baselines

- downloads: CSV, GeoJSON, a printable report and raw detections

The process

1. Cleaning. Low-confidence detections, gas flares and industrial heat sources are removed.

2. Common unit. Fires are counted as "fire days": ~1 km cells with a detection on a local solar day. This is fairer between 1 km MODIS and 375 m VIIRS pixels than raw counts.

3. Conversion chain. NOAA-20 is the reference. Each older satellite is converted using the years it overlapped with a newer one:

- Suomi NPP from its 2018–2026 overlap

- Aqua + Terra MODIS from 2012–2020, before Aqua's orbit drift

- Terra alone for 2000–2002

4. Method contest. Each step picks between four methods (a fixed ratio, a ratio per calendar month, a log-linear fit, quantile mapping). A more complex method is used only if it is clearly better on years hidden from the fit.

5. Validation.

- The 2012 step falls from +199 % to +2 % in Asia, and from +111 % to +5 % in Argentina.

- 3,464 of 3,927 satellite changes across all areas look like ordinary year-to-year change.

- The results agree with NASA GFED5 burned area (r = 0.94 for Asia, 0.97 for Argentina) and with Indonesia's official figures (0.90).

The benefits

- Fire agencies, haze forecasters and researchers get a long-term record that stays trustworthy across sensor changes, with honest uncertainty ranges, down to the district.

- Every number can be traced to a tested step and every method choice is logged in the repository.

What is hope to be achieve

- Extend the record to all of South America and then the world. A compact storage format for this is already built and tested.

- Host the app publicly.

- Add conversions per land type.

- Correct fire counts for fires hidden under thick haze.

Tools used

- Data processing: Python (pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, LightGBM, Shapely, PyArrow, Matplotlib), with 133 automated tests.

- Web app: TypeScript, Next.js and React , MapLibre GL, deck.gl, Recharts, DuckDB-wasm and Tailwind CSS

- Data: NASA FIRMS, NASA GIBS, NASA POWER and GFED5.

- Hardware: a standard 16 GB laptop
